items.raw_content: Hello HN, This is Diego from Krea. Today we are announcing the open beta of Krea 3, our newest foundational image model. In a nutshell, it’s a frontier image model in terms of quality, but at a fraction of the speed and a fraction of the price. We will be releasing a more technical update, like we did with Krea 2 ( https://www.krea.ai/blog/krea-2-technical-report ), but this website shows the capabilities we focused on: * Native regional edits * Precise edits so that there is minimal area degradation pixel-wise * Frontier image quality. In terms of future updates, the team is thinking about letting folks fine-tune Krea 3 (via LoRAs) and open-weights, but

items.title: I know why the mathematicians weep
items.raw_content: In the last few months, OpenAI has stunned the mathematical community with the publication of hundreds of math findings. Many of these proofs, which span number theory, theoretical computer science, and logic, had stumped the world’s best mathematicians for decades, or centuries. The reaction from the math community has been a mix of indignation, astonishment, and sorrow. “Tuesday night, I cried and it woke up my daughter,” said Hugo Duminil-Copin, the recipient of the 2022 Fields Medal, after OpenAI’s October release. “They have annihilated my field of research.”
items.title_zh: 我知道数学家为何哭泣
items.summary: OpenAI has published hundreds of mathematical results in recent months, spanning number theory, theoretical computer science and logic, many of which had gone unsolved for decades or longer, according to this essay. items.title: SlopCodeBench 10/2026 – Opus 5.5, Astra wins overall, xhigh considered harmful
items.raw_content: Quick update here since a lot of folks asked about what slopcodebench is / where it fits in Slop code bench is unique among benchmarks in that it makes a model work against a progressively disclosed list of features (checkpoints) that it doesn’t know it advance, inheriting the same codebase through the lifecycle of a single multi-checkpoint challenge I like this because it much more mirrors how real software dev happens, rather than most benchmarks with one off tasks where slop code doesn’t hinder future progress The original post[1] and the SOL/fable follow up[2] went into a bit more detail on the benchmark and its challenges 1. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49076391 2. https://github.com/humanlayer/advanced-context-engineering-f...

items.title: Graph Serializations for Reasoning LLMs: A Study Across Knowledge Extraction and Structural Reasoning
items.raw_content:
Authors: Julien Yu, Mihaela Bornea, Avirup Sil, Katrin Kirchhoff

The way a knowledge graph is serialized as text for inclusion into LLM context can substantially affect downstream LLM performance, with prior work reporting tens of percentage points variations across formats. However, existing studies consider only a limited set of representations and predate frontier reasoning models, which now offer stronger reasoning, instruction-following, and long-context capabilities. We evaluate 15 graph representation formats across nine frontier LLM configurations on ontology-based knowledge extraction and structural graph reasoning tasks. While knowledge extraction is relatively insensitive to different serialization formats, the choice of the optimal format for structural reasoning tasks significantly affects accuracy. We demonstrate that the optimal representation choice depends on model, query, and task and propose to approach graph serialization as a dynamic orchestration decision.
items.title_zh: 面向推理 LLM 的图序列化：跨知识抽取与结构推理的研究
items.summary: The authors evaluate 15 knowledge-graph serialization formats across nine frontier LLM configurations on ontology-based knowledge extraction and structural graph reasoning tasks. They find extraction is relatively insensitive to format, while structural reasoning accuracy varies significantly, and propose treating serialization as a dynamic orchestration decision.

items.title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing
items.raw_content:
Authors: Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou et al.

Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
items.title_zh: OmniXRef：多模态多参考视频编辑统一框架
items.summary: OmniXRef is a unified framework that lets users combine text, image and video references to control attributes of a source video during editing. It pairs a reference-bank input design and R^2-RoPE with a single-stream diffusion transformer, and introduces the OmniXRef-Data pipeline and OmniXRef-Bench; the authors report gains over task-specific and commercial baselines.

items.title: LEMON: Equivariant Learning over Attention Maps for Zero-Shot Misbehavior Monitoring on New LLMs
items.raw_content:
Authors: Guy Bar-Shalom, Mor Geva, Fabrizio Frasca, Haggai Maron

Large language models exhibit misbehaviors that hinder deployment in high-stakes settings. One approach to monitor such failures is to use an external LLM as a monitor, but this is prohibitively expensive. A well-known and efficient class of monitors can detect such failures from internal representations (such as activation probes), but are tied to the model they were trained on, requiring costly re-annotation as new LLMs appear. A natural way to avoid this repeated annotation cost is to develop internal-representation based monitors that transfer zero-shot across LLMs. However, such transfer is challenging because internal representations are not naturally aligned across models; in particular, attention maps, known to contain signals of misbehavior, may differ in head function, ordering, and model depth. In this work, we characterize those cross-model attention mismatches as algebraic symmetries and use geometric deep learning principles to build LEMON (Language-model Equivariant MOnitoring Network) an online graph neural network-based monitor, whose predictions are invariant under these symmetries. LEMON processes attention maps token-by-token, as they are produced and outputs a score after every token (or every window of $W$ tokens) at negligible cost. Across 16 LLMs and six datasets, in the zero-shot cross-model setting, LEMON outperforms all baselines on both hallucination and jailbreak monitoring tasks, improving over the strongest by up to 14 ROC-AUC points.
items.title_zh: LEMON：基于注意力图等变学习的新 LLM 零样本异常行为监控
items.summary: LEMON is a graph neural network monitor that reads attention maps token by token and is designed to transfer zero-shot across LLMs for hallucination and jailbreak detection. Across 16 LLMs and six datasets it beat all baselines, improving on the strongest by up to 14 ROC-AUC points.

items.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
items.raw_content:
Authors: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas

Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
items.title_zh: LLM-Attack Suite：拆分与分布式 LLM 系统隐私评估的统一红队框架
items.summary: The paper presents LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records attacker assumptions, datasets and scoring rules so privacy evaluations of split and distributed LLM systems can be compared. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding training gradients raised token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%.

items.title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting
items.raw_content:
Authors: Jung Hun Phee, Tucker Balch

We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow. The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty jointly. Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not establish fidelity to the joint field distribution. We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics. In the primary comparison on 1950 validation conditions across 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8% and the transport energy score by 26.1% relative to training with mean squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock. These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty evaluated together.
items.title_zh: OrderFlowDiT：面向限价订单供给概率预测的传输正则化扩散 Transformer
items.summary: The paper introduces OrderFlowDiT, a conditional diffusion transformer trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport loss to forecast bid and ask volume-at-price fields. On 1,950 validation conditions across 30 U.S. equities, adding the loss cut full-field transport cost by 45.8% and the transport energy score by 26.1% versus mean-squared-error training.

items.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
items.raw_content:
Authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Zixiao Chen, Jeevana Priya Inala et al.

Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.
items.title_zh: TokenEconomizer：面向编程智能体的经验驱动黑盒成本控制
items.summary: TokenEconomizer is an external controller that injects micro-skills, prunes persistently irrelevant tools and intervenes in unproductive failure loops to cut token costs for coding agents. Across Claude Code, Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI, it reduced average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success.

items.title: SPADE-KD: Peer-to-Peer Collaborative Learning under Heterogeneous Settings
items.raw_content:
Authors: Harikrishna Kuttivelil, Katia Obraczka

Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.
items.title_zh: SPADE-KD：异构环境下的点对点协作学习
items.summary: SPADE-KD is a fully decentralized distillation framework for peer-to-peer learning that adapts transfer strength to each peer's local performance and selects partners by measured utility. On federated classification tasks it reports lower loss and faster convergence than naive decentralized distillation.

items.title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Measuring Harmful Reachability in Autoregressive Language Models
items.raw_content:
Authors: Parv Kapoor, Teresa Fortes, Claudia Mamede, Rui Abreu, Jonathan Aldrich et al.

LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.
items.title_zh: 拒绝不等于鲁棒：衡量自回归语言模型中的有害可达性
items.summary: The authors introduce bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process and estimates the probability of reaching harmful continuations rather than relying only on sampled attack success rates. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, they report that BCA quantifies hidden harmful behavior and can help direct red-team effort.

items.title: Input- and Feature-Space Correction for Cross-Hospital IHC Grading
items.raw_content:
Authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan

Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
items.title_zh: 跨医院 IHC 分级中的输入空间与特征空间校正
items.summary: The study benchmarks label-free input- and feature-space corrections for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology foundation models UNI and Virchow2. Combining its FIX method with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 by 0.181 and quadratic weighted kappa by 0.208 while reducing ordinal error by 0.209.

items.title: Improving OCR Accuracy Through Multi-Classifier Verification of Visually Similar Characters
items.raw_content:
Authors: Nuzhat Khan, Ab Al-Hadi Ab Rahman, Mohamad Anuar Kamaruddin, Muhammad Paend Bakht, Sana Fatima et al.

Distinguishing visually similar characters is a persistent challenge for optical character recognition (OCR) systems, causing errors in critical applications of text digitization. While preprocessing techniques improve image quality and word-level post-processing corrects spelling errors, neither addresses character-level visual ambiguity, an intrinsic property of certain character pairs that limits even state-of-the-art OCR models. We present the Character Verification Model (CVM), a character-level post-processing framework that verifies and corrects ambiguous characters in OCR outputs using specialized binary classifiers trained on visually confusable pairs such as 'O'/'0', 'Z'/'2', and 'S'/'5'. CVM operates independently of dictionary validation, making it suitable for non-lexical data including serial numbers, alphanumeric codes, and license plates. Experiments on three OCR engines (Tesseract, EasyOCR, TrOCR) and ten fonts with low to high complexity demonstrate accuracy improvements of 3.95-14.81 percentage points, with an 87.3% correction rate for visually similar character errors and a false-correction rate of only 2.3%. The modular architecture integrates with existing OCR pipelines without modification to underlying recognition models.
items.title_zh: 通过多分类器校验视觉相似字符提升 OCR 准确率
items.summary: The paper presents the Character Verification Model, a character-level post-processing step that uses binary classifiers for confusable pairs such as O/0, Z/2 and S/5 without relying on dictionary checks. Across Tesseract, EasyOCR and TrOCR on ten fonts, it improved accuracy by 3.95-14.81 percentage points, with an 87.3% correction rate and a 2.3% false-correction rate.
